rows.timeline_year_basis: The Qur'an is never dated; it is the single starting block
rows.name: Qur'an
rows.detail: No direct verse — jurists cite the shared root darb fi'l-ard (travelling for livelihood) as wording-level support only.
rows.detail_long: Who: The Qur'an is the first rung of every USUL ladder: it is never dated, and every later rung refers back to it. What: Ibn Hazm's verdict stands: qirad rests on consensus, not text. The darb-fi'l-ard verses (73:20, 2:198, 62:10) share vocabulary with mudarabah but legislate nothing about it. The verses, in the translation held in the Gold Ark Library: 2:198 — “There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord [during Hajj]. But when you depart from 'Arafat, remember Allah at al- Mash'ar al-Haram. And remember Him, as He has guided you, for indeed, you were before that among those astray.” 62:10 — “And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse within the land and seek from the bounty of Allah, and remember Allah often that you may succeed.” Why here: The Qur'an opens the Mudarabah ladder and is never dated. Source: Qur'an 73:20; 2:198; 62:10.

rows.name: Prophetic practice (Khadija trade)
rows.detail: The Prophet traded for Khadija on qirad terms before prophethood and later approved the practice.
rows.detail_long: Who: Khadija bint Khuwaylid (555-619), the Prophet's first wife, was a wealthy merchant of Quraysh in her own right. She employed Muhammad to manage a trade caravan to Syria. What: The sira records the young Muhammad trading Khadija's capital for a profit share — mudarabah's living precedent, approved by his later silence and the Companions' practice. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Mudarabah ladder; shown at 610 (pre-prophethood practice, period placement). Source: Prophetic biography (sira) accounts.

rows.name: Sunan Ibn Majah 2289
rows.detail: 'Three things carry blessing: deferred-payment sale, muqaradah (profit-sharing), mixing wheat with barley for the house' — graded Da'eef.
rows.detail_long: Who: Sunan Ibn Majah was compiled by Ibn Majah al-Qazwini (824-887); it is the last of the six canonical Sunni hadith collections. Narrator: Suhayb (via his son Salih). What: The one hadith naming profit-sharing directly — and its grading is Da'eef (weak), so it is support, not proof. Mudarabah's real weight is Companion practice: Umar, Uthman, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and Aisha invested orphans' funds this way. Dated 622-640 CE (medium confidence). The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'There are three things in which there is blessing: A sale with deferred payment; Muqaradhah (profit sharing); and mixing wheat with barley for one's house, but not for sale.” It stands in The Chapter on Business Transactions. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Mudarabah ladder; shown at 622 (dated record in the Gold Ark Library). Source: Sunan Ibn Majah 2289.

rows.display_note: Companion-era investor conditions — the earliest risk covenants on record
rows.name: Bulugh al-Maram 1043
rows.detail: Muqaradah risk conditions. Hakim ibn Hizam's muqaradah covenants: no livestock, no sea transport, no river-bed camps — breach them and you guarantee my capital.
rows.detail_long: Who: Bulugh al-Maram is one of the hadith collections held in the Gold Ark Library. Narrator: al-Hakim bin Hazim (Hakim ibn Hizam). What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: capital handed over for muqaradah (profit shared) under named prohibitions — trading in living beings, carrying it by sea, settling at a river bottom — with liability shifting to the agent on breach. Investor risk restrictions and a breach-triggers-guarantee clause, in the first generation. The direct ancestor of every mudarabah investment-restriction schedule. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “He used to make a condition on the man to whom he gave his property in al-Muqaradah (to trade with, and the profit being shared between them), that: "You should not trade with my property in living beings, and do not transport it by sea, and do not settle with it at the bottom of a river-bed; and if you do any of the aforesaid acts you should then guarantee my property." .” It stands in Business Transactions. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Mudarabah ladder; shown at 622 (dated 622-632 (Madinan period); shown at the earliest year). Source: Bulugh al-Maram 1043.

rows.name: Mishkat al-Masabih 2815
rows.detail: Muqarada among the blessed things. Muqarada named among blessed practices: deferred-term sale, muqarada, and mixing wheat with barley for the household, not for sale.
rows.detail_long: Who: Mishkat al-Masabih is one of the hadith collections held in the Gold Ark Library. Narrator: Suhaib. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library (Suhaib; Ibn Majah transmitted): the record lists muqarada with its own gloss — 'giving someone some property to trade with, the profit being shared between the two, but any loss falling on the property.' Profit shared, loss on capital: the mudarabah loss rule stated inside the hadith corpus itself. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “A business transaction with a time specified, muqarada* and mixing wheat and barley for one’s household but not for sale.” Ibn Majah transmitted it. * Giving someone some property to trade with, the profit being shared between the two, but any loss falling on the property.” It stands in Business Transactions. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Mudarabah ladder; shown at 622 (dated 622-632 (Madinan period); shown at the earliest year). Source: Mishkat al-Masabih 2815.

rows.timeline_year_basis: Dated 622-632, medium confidence; shown at the earliest year; the content reports the judge Shuraih (first Islamic century)
rows.display_note: Graded Sahih. Bridge row: the hadith corpus recording COURT practice on mudarabah
rows.name: Sunan an-Nasa'i 3967

hadith_meta.narrator: Muhammad (ibn Sirin), on the judge Shuraih

rows.detail: Shuraih's two rulings on mudarabah disputes. Judge Shuraih's complete mudarabah case law: the agent proves calamity to be excused; the investor proves betrayal, else the agent's oath stands.
rows.detail_long: Who: The Sunan of al-Nasa'i (829-915), a noted collector of hadith from the city of Nasa, is one of the six canonical Sunni hadith collections. Narrator: Muhammad (ibn Sirin), on the judge Shuraih. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: 'I do not know that Shuraih ever ruled on Mudarabah disputes except in two ways' — burden of proof on the mudarib for loss-by-calamity, burden on the investor for breach-of-trust, the agent's oath sufficing otherwise. Evidence law for profit-sharing disputes, already settled in the first century and preserved with a Sahih grading. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “It was narrated that Muhammad said: I do not know that Shuraih ever ruled on Mudarabah disputes except in two ways. He would say to the Mudarib (the one who contributed his labor to the partnership): 'You must provide proof that a calamity befell you so that you may be excused.' Or he would say to the one who invested his money in the partnership: 'You must provide proof that your trustee betrayed his trust, otherwise his oath sworn by Allah that he did not betray you is sufficient.” It stands in The Book of Agriculture. Why here: 'Early judicial practice' rung of the Mudarabah ladder; shown at 622 (dated 622-632, medium confidence; shown at the earliest year; the content reports the judge Shuraih (first Islamic century)). Source: Sunan an-Nasa'i 3967.

rows.display_note: The founding case: retroactive qirad, principal + half profit to the treasury
rows.name: Muwatta 1450

hadith_meta.narrator: Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father

rows.detail: Umar converts his sons' windfall into qirad. Abu Musa lends state money to Umar's sons; they trade and profit; Umar rules it qirad — treasury takes principal plus half the profit.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Muwatta is the work of Malik ibn Anas (711-795), the jurist of Medina and eponym of the Maliki school. Narrator: Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: the sons of Umar carry public funds from Basra, buy Iraqi wares, sell in Madina at profit. Umar objects that the loan came only because of who they were; Ubaydullah answers that they bore the guarantee had it perished. A bystander proposes: 'make it a qirad.' Umar does — principal and half-profit to the treasury, half-profit to the traders. The canonical origin case for capital-labour profit splitting. The report (opening), as held in the Gold Ark Library: “Malik related to me from Zayd ibn Aslam that his father said, "Abdullah and Ubaydullah, the sons of Umar ibn al-Khattab went out with the army to Iraq. On the way home, they passed by Abu Musa al- Ashari who was the amir of Basra. He greeted them and made them welcome, and told them that if there was anything he could do to help them, he would do it. Then he said, 'There is some of the property of Allah which I want to send to the amir al-muminin, so I will lend it to you, and you can buy wares from Iraq and sell them in Madina. [...]” It stands in Qirad. Why here: 'Companion practice' rung of the Mudarabah ladder; shown at 632 (dated 632-661 (dated by the Companion named in the report: Umar ibn al-Khattab); shown at the earliest year). Source: Muwatta 1450, Qirad chapter.

rows.name: Muwatta 1451

hadith_meta.narrator: al-Ala ibn Abd ar-Rahman, from his father, from his father

rows.detail: Uthman gives money as qirad. Uthman ibn Affan gives capital as qirad on profit-sharing terms — a second caliph practising the contract.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Muwatta is the work of Malik ibn Anas (711-795), the jurist of Medina and eponym of the Maliki school. Narrator: al-Ala ibn Abd ar-Rahman, from his father, from his father. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: 'Uthman ibn Affan gave him some money as qirad to use provided the profit was shared between them.' One line, but a caliph-level precedent independent of Umar's case. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “Malik related to me from al-Ala ibn Abd ar-Rahman from his father from his father that Uthman ibn Affan gave him some money as qirad to use provided the profit was shared between them.” It stands in Qirad. Why here: 'Companion practice' rung of the Mudarabah ladder; shown at 632 (dated 632-661 (dated by the Companion named in the report: Uthman); shown at the earliest year). Source: Muwatta 1451, Qirad chapter.

hadith_meta.narrator: abu al-Sabbah al-Kinani, from Imam al-Sadiq
topics_app: Liability for Profit Sharing, Its Profit and Expenses (Al-Mudarabah)

rows.detail: Mudarabah liability chapter. Imam al-Sadiq: the working partner takes his profit share but bears no loss — unless he violates the owner's instructions.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Kafi was compiled by al-Kulayni (864-941), a Persian Shia scholar and hadith compiler. Narrator: abu al-Sabbah al-Kinani, from Imam al-Sadiq. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library, from a chapter titled 'Liability for Profit Sharing, Its Profit and Expenses (Al-Mudarabah)': the mudarib 'can have (his share of) the profit but is not liable for depreciation (loss) unless he violates the instructions of the owner of the assets.' The same loss-on-capital / breach-shifts-liability structure as the Sunni line — stated from the Imami side. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “7. Abu Ali al-Ash’ariy has narrated from Muhammad ibn ‘Abd al-Jabbar from Muhammad ibn ‘Isma’il from Ali ibn al-Nu’man from abu al-Sabbah al-Kinaniy who has said the following: “About the case of a man who works for Mudarabah (profit sharing), abu ‘Abd Allah (a.s.), has said, ‘He can have (his share of) the profit but is not liable for depreciation (loss) unless he violates the instructions of the owner of the assets.”’” It stands in Liability for Profit Sharing, Its Profit and Expenses ( Al-Mudarabah ). Why here: 'Imami reports (Shia line)' rung of the Mudarabah ladder; shown at 941 (compilation date: al-Kulayni (d.941, standard reference); report attributed to Imam al-Sadiq). Source: Al-Kafi vol.5, hadith 890.

rows.name: Malik ibn Anas
rows.detail: Malik's al-Muwatta, Book of Qirad — the earliest systematic record, with Uthman's qirad deal and Umar's sons trading public money.
rows.detail_long: Who: Malik ibn Anas (711-795), called the Imam of Medina, is the eponym of the Maliki school, one of the four Sunni schools of law; the school became the norm in much of North Africa and al-Andalus. Al-Muwatta is his work. Al-Shafi'i was his best-known student. What: Kitab al-Qirad preserves the founding cases: Uthman funding a trader for half the profit, and Umar converting his sons' windfall into the first recorded qirad ruling. The Muwatta's Qirad chapter: 1452 defines the recognised qirad (no guarantee by the agent; travel food/clothing from capital when it can bear it); 1453 disapproves converting an unpaid debt into qirad before repossession — 'the debtor may be in a tight situation, and want to delay it to increase it'; 1455 bans either party stipulating any exclusive gain — 'no sale, no rent, no work, no advance' reserved to one side without the other sharing. Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Mudarabah ladder, Maliki voice; shown at 795 (year of the author's death). Source: Al-Muwatta, Kitab al-Qirad.

rows.name: al-Sarakhsi
rows.detail: Al-Sarakhsi's al-Mabsut gives the fullest early Hanafi treatment of mudarabah.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Sarakhsi (1009-1090) was a jurist of the Hanafi school, traditionally known as Shams al-A'imma ('Sun of the Imams'); a saying of the school runs 'when in doubt, follow Sarakhsi'. He is said to have written al-Mabsut while imprisoned. Later Hanafi works, including al-Kasani's Bada'i al-Sana'i, draw heavily on it. What: The Mabsut's mudarabah book works through capital conditions, permitted manager actions and profit-split rules — the systematic Hanafi doctrine. In the work itself (near vol. and page 22:17; our literal translation from the Arabic): “And the people of Madina call this contract muqarada, and that is narrated from 'Uthman - may God be pleased with him - for he handed over wealth to a man as muqarada.” It also states: “God, exalted is He, said: {and others who strike [travel] in the land seeking of the bounty of God} [al-Muzzammil: 20], meaning travel for trade. And the permissibility of this contract is known by the Sunna and consensus.” It also states: “[Of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, when he handed over wealth as mudaraba:] he stipulated on the mudarib that he not travel a sea with it, and that he not descend a valley, and not buy with it a possessor of a moist liver; and if he did that, he is liable.” Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Mudarabah ladder, Hanafi voice; shown at 1090 (year of the author's death). Source: Al-Mabsut.

rows.name: al-Kasani
rows.detail: Al-Kasani: strict analogy would forbid mudarabah — it stands on consensus and need.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Kasani (d. 587 AH / 1191 CE) was a jurist of the Hanafi school and author of Bada'i al-Sana'i, a work that draws heavily on al-Sarakhsi's al-Mabsut. What: Bada'i concedes qiyas would void mudarabah (undefined labor for undefined wage) and validates it by ijma' and people's need — the classic case of consensus overriding analogy. In the work itself (vol. and page 6:79; our literal translation from the Arabic): “(As for) the first [the permissibility of this contract], analogy is that it is not permissible; because it is a hiring for an unknown wage - rather for a non-existent wage - and for unknown work; but we left analogy because of the Mighty Book and the Sunna and consensus.” It also states: “{And others who strike [travel] in the land seeking of the bounty of God} [al-Muzzammil: 20]; and the mudarib strikes [travels] in the land seeking of the bounty of God.” It also states: “[From the report cited from Ibn 'Abbas about al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib when he handed over wealth as mudaraba:] he stipulated on his counterpart that he not travel a sea with it, nor descend a valley with it, nor buy with it an animal possessing a moist liver; and if he did that, he is liable.” It also states: “And what counts in contracts is their meanings, not the forms of the words.” Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Mudarabah ladder, Hanafi voice; shown at 1191 (standard references). Source: Bada'i al-Sana'i.

rows.name: Ibn Qudama al-Maqdisi
rows.detail: Ibn Qudama treats mudarabah extensively for the Hanbalis.
rows.detail_long: Who: Ibn Qudama al-Maqdisi (1147-1223) was a jurist of the Hanbali school who studied in Baghdad and taught in Damascus; he is regarded as one of the school's most authoritative classical figures. He is best known for al-Mughni, a legal encyclopedia that compares the opinions of the Sunni schools while setting out the Hanbali position in detail. He also wrote 'Umdat al-Fiqh. What: Al-Mughni's treatment covers capital, management and loss rules for the Hanbali school. In the work itself (vol. and page 5:19; our literal translation from the Arabic): “(3642) Section: the third division, that a body and wealth share. And this is mudaraba, and it is also called qirad; and its meaning is that a man hands over his wealth to another who trades for him with it, on the basis that what results of profit is between the two of them according to what they stipulate.” It also states: “So the people of Iraq call it mudaraba, taken from striking [travelling] in the land, and it is travel in it for trade. God, exalted is He, said: {and others who strike [travel] in the land seeking of the bounty of God} [al-Muzzammil: 20].” It also states: “And the people of knowledge agreed on the permissibility of mudaraba in general. Ibn al-Mundhir mentioned it.” It also states: “[Reported from Humayd ibn 'Abd Allah, from his father, from his grandfather:] that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab gave him an orphan's wealth as mudaraba, to work with it in Iraq.” Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Mudarabah ladder, Hanbali voice; shown at 1223 (year of the author's death). Source: Al-Mughni.

rows.name: Yahya ibn Sharif al-Nawawi
rows.detail: Al-Nawawi gives a full book to qirad: it 'exists between two persons, one of whom supplies funds to the other to trade with', on condition of a share in the profit.
rows.detail_long: Who: Yahya ibn Sharaf al-Nawawi (1233-1277), known as Muhyi al-Din, was a Shafi'i jurist and hadith scholar of Damascus. His works include Minhaj al-Talibin and Riyad al-Salihin; al-Asnawi described him as the editor and refiner of the Shafi'i school. What: The standard Shafi'i manual treats mudarabah under the name qirad (Howard's English calls it a 'joint-stock company'): one party funds, the other trades, and the funder shares the profit. Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Mudarabah ladder, Shafi'i voice; shown at 1277 (year of the author's death). Source: Minhaj al-Talibin, Book 19 (Qirad).

rows.name: al-Tabari
rows.detail: Commentary attaches to the darb-fi'l-ard verses but treats the link as wording only, not legal proof.
rows.detail_long: Who: Abu Ja'far al-Tabari (839-923) was a Sunni scholar, historian, jurist and Qur'an commentator from Amol in Tabaristan who worked in Baghdad. He followed the Shafi'i school for nearly a decade, then developed his own school of law (the Jariri school), which lasted about two centuries after him. He is best known for his Qur'an commentary, Tafsir al-Tabari (Jami' al-Bayan), and his historical chronicle. What: Al-Tabari on 73:20 reads 'others travelling the land seeking Allah's bounty' as those journeying for trade and earnings — vocabulary shared with mudarabah, but no contract ruling drawn from it. Confirms the contract's basis lies in practice and consensus, not this verse. Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Mudarabah ladder; shown at 923 (year of the author's death). Source: Jami' al-Bayan (Tafsir al-Tabari), on Q73:20.

rows.name: Mohammad Nejatullah Siddiqi
rows.work_title: Partnership and Profit-Sharing in Islamic Law
rows.detail: Siddiqi's 'Partnership and Profit-Sharing in Islamic Law' — the seminal modern theory; basis of two-tier deposit banking.
rows.detail_long: Who: Mohammad Nejatullah Siddiqi (1931-2022) was an Indian economist (Aligarh; King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah), winner of the King Faisal Prize in 1982 and known for the two-tier mudarabah banking model. What: Siddiqi formalizes mudarabah as the engine of interest-free banking: depositors as rabb al-mal, the bank as mudarib, then the bank re-deploying funds as rabb al-mal — the two-tier model every Islamic bank charter cites. In the source's own words (Penn Libraries catalogue record - Partnership and profit-sharing in Islamic law / Muhammad Nejatullah Siddiqi): “Place of Publication: Leicester, UK : Islamic Foundation, [1985]” “Series: Islamic economic series ; 9. Physical Description: 111 pages ; 22 cm.” “Subjects (All): Partnership (Islamic law). Profit-sharing--Law and legislation. Profit-sharing.” “Islamic Foundation, c1985" ... "Translated from the Urdu" ... "Reprint of the 1985 ed.” Not confirmed by the source read: No record read gives a table of contents or a description of the book. Nothing read calls it 'the seminal modern theory' or 'basis of two-tier deposit banking'. The King Faisal Prize page does not name 'Partnership and Profit-Sharing in Islamic Law'; it names 'Banking Without Interest' and other titles. Why here: 'Modern rules & standards' rung of the Mudarabah ladder; shown at 1985 (publication year). Source: Siddiqi's 'Partnership and Profit-Sharing in Islamic Law'.

rows.name: AAOIFI
rows.detail: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 13 codifies mudarabah (investment and savings deposits).
rows.detail_long: Who: AAOIFI (the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions) issues the Shari'ah Standards. They are mandatory in Bahrain, its home jurisdiction, and adopted in the UAE and other countries. What: SS13 sets capital, profit-distribution and loss rules for deposit-side mudarabah. Adopted 16 May 2002. Clauses read in the standard's text: 8/8 the mudarib's profit share arises once profit is realised, subject to retention rules; the mudarib bears no losses except on breach of trust — misconduct, negligence or breach of the mudarabah terms; 9/1 in unrestricted mudarabah the mudarib may do what entrepreneurs in his field do; guarantees from the mudarib may cover only negligence, misconduct or breach. Why here: 'Modern rules & standards' rung of the Mudarabah ladder; shown at 2002 (adopted Shari'ah Board meeting 8, Al-Madinah, 28 Safar-4 Rabi' I 1423 / 11-16 May 2002). Source: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 13.

rows.name: Industry practice
rows.detail: Mudarabah survives mainly on the deposit side (investment accounts) and in sukuk; pure two-tier mudarabah banking remains rare.
rows.detail_long: Who: This rung is a snapshot of how the contract is used in the market today. It is a description of practice, not a ruling. What: Modern usage: unrestricted investment accounts (bank as mudarib), mudarabah sukuk, and fund structures — while financing-side mudarabah stays thin because of the no-collateral, no-guaranteed-return core. Why here: 'Where it stands today' rung of the Mudarabah ladder; shown at 2024 (current period marker (2024)). Source: Industry practice (descriptive).
